===== NEW MESSAGES SINCE YOUR LAST TURN =====
**Codex (Backend / Systems Engineer · Systems Thinker) — Round 1**

I’d lock the architecture as a pure local, SwiftUI-first app with a thin domain core and strict state ownership: a single `@Observable` `GameEngine` that owns canonical Klondike logic and a live board state, plus separate `StatsLogStore` and `SettingsStore` services that are restored and persisted independently. That gives you the required three-screen separation (Game/Stats/Settings) without hidden state coupling and prevents a bad game save from breaking stats/settings recovery.

For framework choice, stay strictly on Apple frameworks only: SwiftUI for all screens and overlays, Foundation for Codable models and file I/O, Observation for reactivity, `DispatchQueue`/`Task` for async disk work, and UIKit haptics (`UIImpactFeedbackGenerator`, `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator`) for tactile events. No networking frameworks are needed for this build; avoid URLSession entirely. `SwiftData` is unnecessary given the locked three-file persistence contract; `Codable` + `FileManager` in Application Support is the cleanest and most testable fit here. Keep the file path abstraction behind a protocol so persistence can be tested with temp directories.

The persistence model should be exactly three independent persisted artifacts: `GameSave.json`, `StatsLog.json`, `Settings.json`, each with its own version stamp and atomic write path (`encode -> temp file -> flush -> atomic replace`). This is not just a design choice; it is the reliability boundary: one corrupt file must not block the others. Persist only logical game state and never transient animation offsets. Ensure every restore path is explicit and classified into success, fallback/default, and data-loss states so the UI can show the non-blocking recovery banner instead of pretending old state was valid.

For state shape, define pure value-model types (no UI types in model) with deterministic move rules and replayable undo metadata; this is the testability anchor. `GameState` should be serializable as compact, versioned JSON. Save points should be event-driven (startup, game mutation that settles state, explicit end-of-game, settings updates, timer start/stop) and include minimal metadata for compatibility/migration checks. Add a compact schema field in each file so corrupted or older data can be replaced cleanly.

Offline behavior should be explicit in the architecture: no network calls, no sign-in, no backend adapters, no sync jobs, no background fetch, no push, and no silent server fallback. Use `scenePhase` and app lifecycle hooks only to pause/resume timer state as already decided. When restoring, do one cold-boot pass only; once loaded, the app should be fully functional with airplane mode or offline launch and keep full playability. If restore is impossible, start fresh immediately and proceed with game UI.

Privacy/perms surface should be minimal and stable: there are no user-data collection permissions required, no photos/camera/microphone/location/trackable IDs needed, and no background modes. If the future optional share image flow is deferred (as currently locked out), no photo library or share destination write access is currently needed. Add an explicit settings disclosure line in text about local-only persistence, as already required. Haptics use no privacy impact. Ensure launch and tab screens do not request any permissions.

StoreKit/subscriptions: do not introduce any StoreKit dependency now. This phase should produce explicit non-monetized architecture (`no IAP`, `no ads`, no entitlements, no server-signed purchase flow). If product asks for it later, it should be a phase split and separate contract; otherwise remove all dead code branches (product identifiers, receipt verification, paywall screens) so they cannot regress in.

Dependency/licensing risk is therefore zero by default: no third-party package, no SwiftPM additions, no vendored libraries. This directly satisfies the permissive dependency policy and avoids license review risk. The only imported non-Apple packages would be `none`. Keep it that way until after a version 1.0 parity milestone; if a helper dependency is proposed later, require one-line necessity/benefit plus replacement plan.

Testability should be design-first: treat this as testable by construction. Split into protocol-backed services for RNG and persistence, inject a fixed random generator only in tests, and a mock clock for timer pause/resume and draw-mode timing assertions. Unit-test rules thoroughly (single/multi-card run legality, draw-1/draw-3 moves, exact undo restore, stuck detection, win condition), persistence tests for atomic writes + corrupted file fallback, and lifecycle tests for background pause and relaunch state consistency. Then add UI tests for core user paths: resume launch, new game/new game confirmation, move accepted/blocked feedback, win/stuck overlays, mode switching confirmation, and draw mode stats segregation per mode. Accessibility-focused UI assertions should verify CardView labels/actions and no control overlap in the target layouts.

The strongest risk I’d call out in this architecture is migration/restore ambiguity under crash timing: if you write partially during animations or combine UI and logical writes, you get “looks corrupted” states despite valid game logic. Preserve this by committing only settled logical state from the core engine to persistence, and by treating save/restores as synchronous contracts in the engine layer before SwiftUI sees them. Also preserve the finality rule that card colors, fonts, and spacing come from a single `Theme.swift` token source so accidental literals don’t reintroduce visual-policy drift.

**Claude (QA & Risk · Closer) — Round 1**

Picking up where design_handoff left off, my job here is to turn "here's a beautiful numeric spec" into "here's what actually ships without silently violating a decision already on the books" — so I'm going to name the specific architecture gaps and lock a position on each rather than flag them as open questions for someone else.

Architecture: iOS 17 minimum, SwiftUI-only view layer, one `@Observable` `GameEngine` class owning board/undo/timer state instantiated once at the App root and injected via `@Environment`, exactly as design_handoff specified — I have nothing to add there, it's sound. What I want to nail down is persistence, because the locked decision (three independent files, FileManager, atomic temp-then-swap, no SwiftData, no encryption) is a real deviation from this fleet's stated default of "prefer SwiftData first," and if tech_specs doesn't restate that deviation explicitly with its justification, someone downstream will "fix" it back to SwiftData and quietly reopen a decision that took three rounds to close. The justification is legitimate — this data has no query needs, no relationships, no large record counts, and SwiftData's migration/schema machinery is pure overhead for three small Codable structs — but it needs to be written into tech_specs as an explicit, intentional exception with a one-line rationale, not left implicit.

Two gaps I don't think any earlier phase actually closed, and I want to close them now instead of letting them surface as bugs during build. First: undo history persistence. Every phase locked "multi-step undo" and "persist logical state across backgrounding and relaunch," but nobody said whether the undo *stack itself* survives an app kill, or only the current board position does. If it doesn't survive, a player who backgrounds mid-hand and gets jetsam-killed comes back to a board that looks identical but has silently lost their undo history — which is exactly the kind of quiet data-integrity lie this app's whole positioning is against. I'm locking it: the undo stack is part of `GameSave.json`, capped at a generous bound (200 entries is more than any real game needs) purely to bound file size, not because deep undo is discouraged. Second gap: save cadence. "Atomic write" says *how* we persist, not *when*. `scenePhase` transitioning to `.background` is necessary but not sufficient — a hard jetsam kill or crash while foregrounded won't fire that callback, and this app has zero excuse to lose a move that already resolved. So: persist after every state-mutating event (move, undo, stock draw), coalesced/debounced by roughly 300-500ms so a rapid sequence of taps doesn't thrash disk, plus an unconditional flush on `scenePhase` background. Both save paths write through one serial `PersistenceActor` per file so a coalesced background write can never race a foreground write and interleave into a corrupted temp-swap.

On the legibility gate that every single phase so far has flagged as untested and unresolved — I don't want to hand that off again as an "open risk" for the fourth time in a row. I'm proposing the concrete mechanism that actually closes it: a debug-only SwiftUI preview or in-app hidden gallery view that renders all 52 `CardView`s at the real computed `cardWidth` formula output side by side, so a human can actually eyeball it once at true device scale before the glyph `Shape` paths are treated as final — this needs to exist as a build artifact, not a promise. If it fails, the fallback order is: simplify the glyph first, increase stroke weight/contrast second, only touch the sizing formula last, since the formula is what protects seven-column portrait layout.

RNG and testability: production shuffle stays `Array.shuffled()` off the system generator, full stop, per the already-locked no-second-RNG-path decision. But `GameEngine`'s deal function should take an injectable `RandomNumberGenerator` as a default parameter defaulting to the system one — that's a pure testing seam, lets unit tests build deterministic, reproducible board fixtures (including hand-constructed adversarial draw-3 boards for stuck-detection false-positive testing), and it must never be reachable from any UI or production code path. I want that constraint stated explicitly in tech_specs so nobody "helpfully" wires a debug menu to it later and reopens the seeded-replay question that was already killed for a good reason.

Testing strategy, concretely, because "add tests" isn't a plan: unit tests over `GameEngine` for every legality rule (foundation ascending/same-suit, tableau alternating-descending, King-to-empty-only, run-relocation validity), win detection, both stuck-detection paths, and undo restoring exact struct equality, not just "looks right." On top of that, a randomized simulation test — a bot playing thousands of legal moves across both draw modes per CI run — asserting invariants that would catch a whole class of bugs no hand-written test will: always exactly 52 unique cards accounted for, foundations never exceed rank 13, stuck-detection never fires while `canMove` finds a legal move anywhere on the board. That last one is the actual test that makes DEC-app_features-002's "never falsely declare stuck" promise real instead of aspirational. XCUITest coverage for the observable flows: cold-launch deal completing into an interactive board, blocked-move feedback, both confirmation-sheet paths, and the two structurally-distinct Stats states actually rendering differently. And since this is a fully custom-rendered UI with no system `List`/`Form` chrome, none of it gets automatic accessibility identifiers or VoiceOver behavior — every `CardView`, `WinOverlay`/`StuckOverlay`, and confirmation sheet needs explicit `.accessibilityIdentifier` for UI-test hooks and explicit labels/traits for VoiceOver, and I'd run Xcode's built-in `performAccessibilityAudit()` inside the UI test suite, since it's a real API that catches contrast/label/hit-target issues for free and this fleet has a documented history of shipping custom-rendered screens that quietly break accessibility.

Permissions and privacy: there are none. No camera, location, contacts, photo library, microphone, network — zero `Info.plist` usage-description keys, zero entitlements beyond the app sandbox default, zero background modes declared (the timer-pause-on-background requirement needs no `BGTaskScheduler` or background execution entitlement at all, just `scenePhase` observation while foregrounded). The one thing that's easy to miss and is a hard App Store submission requirement regardless of how privacy-clean the app is: Apple now requires a `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy` manifest declaring any "required-reason API" usage, and `FileManager`/`UserDefaults` both fall under that depending on exactly which APIs get called. I'd resolve this by keeping all persistence on `FileManager` + Application Support directory only, not `UserDefaults` at all, which narrows the required-reason surface to one well-understood category instead of two, and the manifest still needs to be authored and shipped even though the honest answer to every tracking/data-collection question in it is "no."

StoreKit: zero code, zero capability, confirmed non-goal, nothing to design here — I'm stating it explicitly so tech_specs doesn't leave a gap that reads as "undecided" versus "deliberately absent." Dependencies: zero third-party packages, and given this fleet's own documented history of shipping dependency-lint failures, I want an actual CI-checkable gate, not just a policy statement — a build step that fails if `Package.resolved` (or the Xcode project's package references) contains anything beyond the app's own targets. Concurrency: `GameEngine` is main-actor-isolated since every mutation is UI-driven; persistence I/O runs through the serial `PersistenceActor` off the main actor so a coalesced disk write never stalls a spring animation frame.

None of this should be controversial enough to need a second round from my side — the only place I expect pushback is the undo-persists-through-kill call and the save-cadence trigger, since neither was explicitly locked earlier, but I think the data-integrity argument for both is airtight given this app's whole premise is not lying to the player about their own state.

**Coordinator (Claude) — decision after round 1**

**CONSENSUS: NO**

Here's where round 1 landed. Codex laid down the architecture skeleton — SwiftUI-only, one `@Observable GameEngine` plus separate `StatsLogStore`/`SettingsStore`, Apple frameworks exclusively (SwiftUI, Foundation, Observation, UIKit haptics), Codable+FileManager over SwiftData (since there's no query/relationship need), three atomically-written independent files, zero permissions/StoreKit/dependencies, and a testability plan built around protocol-backed RNG/persistence seams plus unit/persistence/lifecycle/UI test layers. Claude didn't push back on any of that — she explicitly endorsed it as sound and spent her turn extending it into several concrete resolutions nobody had locked yet: the undo stack should persist inside `GameSave.json` (capped at 200 entries) rather than silently vanish on a jetsam kill; save cadence needs to be event-driven (after every state-mutating move, debounced ~300-500ms) plus an unconditional flush on backgrounding, routed through one serial `PersistenceActor` per file to avoid write races; the still-unresolved card-glyph legibility gate needs an actual build artifact — a debug-only gallery view rendering all 52 `CardView`s at the real computed `cardWidth` — not another promise to check later; a `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy` manifest is required even with zero data collection because `FileManager`/`UserDefaults` fall under Apple's required-reason API rules, and she'd narrow that surface by keeping persistence on `FileManager` only (no `UserDefaults`); and she wants a CI-checkable gate (not just a policy line) that fails the build if any third-party package reference shows up.

None of this contradicts Codex — it's additive, and Claude even flagged which parts she expects might get pushback (the undo-persists-through-kill call and the save-cadence trigger, since neither was explicitly locked in an earlier phase). But Codex hasn't seen or responded to any of it yet, so I'm not calling this converged after one side talks. Round 2 needs Codex to explicitly confirm (or contest) Claude's five additions — undo-in-save-file, event-driven+debounced save cadence via a serial actor, the legibility gallery artifact, the FileManager-only/xcprivacy-manifest approach, and the CI dependency-lint gate — before this phase can close.

response:
Codex, reading your round 1 again more carefully, I think we're actually closer than the coordinator gave us credit for — you already wrote "replayable undo metadata" as part of the serializable `GameState`, which is functionally the same call I made explicitly (undo lives inside `GameSave.json`, not just current board position), and you already said save points should be "event-driven (startup, game mutation that settles state, explicit end-of-game, settings updates, timer start/stop)," which is my event-driven cadence too. So let's not treat those as open — they're converged, just say it out loud: undo history persists as part of `GameSave.json`, capped at 200 entries, and saves fire on every settling mutation, not just on background. The one thing I'll add on top of what you wrote: those event-driven writes need to be debounced by a few hundred milliseconds, because "game mutation that settles state" can fire in a tight burst — think a run-relocation move that internally resolves several card position updates, or a rapid sequence of stock draws — and writing to disk synchronously on every one of those is wasted I/O and a stutter risk during exactly the spring animations we're trying to protect. Debounce the write, not the mutation — the in-memory `GameEngine` state updates instantly for the UI, only the disk flush lags by ~300-500ms, with an unconditional non-debounced flush on `scenePhase` background so we never lose more than that window even in a worst-case jetsam kill mid-foreground.

On the async disk work mechanism — you said `DispatchQueue`/`Task`, I want to be more specific and argue for a Swift `actor`, one instance per file (three actors total, not one shared actor serializing all three), rather than raw `DispatchQueue`. The reason to be precise here isn't pedantry: the entire point of the three-file split is that a corrupt or slow write to `GameSave.json` can never block or corrupt `StatsLog.json` or `Settings.json` — if we route all three through one shared queue or one shared actor, we've reintroduced exactly the coupling the three-file design exists to avoid, just moved from disk to the write-scheduling layer. Three independent actors, each serializing only its own file's temp-write-then-atomic-swap, keeps the independent-failure guarantee true end to end, not just at the file-format level. This is the kind of detail that's cheap to get right now in tech_specs and annoying to retrofit after someone's already written `PersistenceManager.shared.save(_:)` as one chokepoint.

I also want to push back gently on leaving the legibility gallery as implied rather than required — you didn't mention it in your round 1 at all, and I think that's the single most consequential gap between our two messages, because it's the one requirement four consecutive earlier phases flagged as unresolved and none of them produced an actual verification mechanism, just another paragraph promising it matters. I'm not asking for agreement on aesthetics, I'm asking for agreement that a specific artifact must exist in the codebase — a debug-reachable view or `#Preview` that renders all 52 `CardView`s at the real `cardWidth` formula output, because without that artifact "check legibility before locking the glyph shapes" is not a testable requirement, it's a hope. If you disagree with the mechanism, propose a different one, but I don't think "we'll know it when we see it" is acceptable for a decision that's been explicitly named a release-blocking gate five times now.

Two more things I want on the record since they weren't in either of our round-1 messages and both are real App Store submission risks, not hypotheticals: no ML or AR of any kind is in scope, so there's no CoreML/CreateML/ARKit/Vision framework anywhere in this build, and I want that stated as a deliberate exclusion rather than an absence nobody noticed — it forecloses a "could we add a smart-hint solver" idea from sneaking in later as scope creep disguised as a technical enhancement. And since there's genuinely zero tracking of any kind, this app never triggers the App Tracking Transparency prompt and needs no `NSUserTrackingUsageDescription` — but I'd explicitly call that out in tech_specs too, because ATT is one of those things engineers sometimes add reflexively "just in case," and every unnecessary permission prompt in a zero-permission app is a bug, not caution.

So here's what I think closes this phase cleanly: your architecture skeleton stands as-is, my five additions from round 1 are confirmed rather than contested (you'd already independently agreed with two of them in your own wording), with the one refinement that saves are debounced-not-synchronous and persistence runs through three independent per-file actors rather than one shared queue, plus the legibility gallery view is locked as a required build artifact and ML/AR plus ATT are stated as explicit, deliberate non-requirements. I don't see a real disagreement left standing between us — if you're fine with the actor-per-file framing and the gallery-as-artifact requirement, I think we're done here without needing a third round.
